new_statements.quote: Stress is nonphonemic. With words in isolation it occurs on the first syllable of two-syllable words and on the second syllable of words of three or more syllables. This consistent behavior of stress has been a primary factor in the analysis of the syllabic nasal and makes it considerably easier for the unpracticed ear to spot many double nasals or vowels word initially.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Non-contrastive word stress on the second syllable of words of three or more syllables; disyllables are stressed on the first syllable (i.e. peninitial with avoidance of final stress). Brown 2025 (already the catalog's primary for Naasioi) restates this in moras: second mora from the left, initial in bimoraic words, long vowels counting as two moras. Rausch 1912 (older Nasioi description, Koromira/Kieta area) instead treats accent as contrastive with minimal pairs and describes a pitch realization (accented syllable and all preceding syllables high, following ones low); his pairs are plausibly unmarked vowel-length differences.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in Hurd & Hurd; the catalog's Brown 2025 record says no secondary stress (acoustic).
new_statements.exceptions: None in this passage beyond the disyllable case. Rausch 1912 notes some disyllables with both syllables on the same pitch level ('dua Sonne, karaṅ Krebs, mutu blind, apo Regen') and 'generally very weak' stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Words in isolation ('With words in isolation'); citation forms. The statement is for Naasioi Proper (Pirung dialect, Darutue village), not for Oune; no Oune data exist in any opened source.
new_statements.identity_note: Ounge [oung1239, ISO oue] is the same entity as Oune (also spelled Aunge; alt. name Dapera); the ISO reference name went Oune -> Ounge (CR 2008-005) -> Oune (CR 2010-024), both filed by Conrad Hurd. Hurd, who has studied Naasioi since 1964 and has visited the Oune villages, states first-hand that Oune 'is but a dialect of Naasioi' (CR 2008-005, Sources (a)) and lists it as one of eight Naasioi dialects (Hurd & Hurd 2020, fn. 1); Tryon 2005: 42 concurs ('perhaps best considered.. dialects of Nasioi'). Naasioi is naas1242, already in the catalog (Brown 2025 primary; Hurd OPD 1992 supporting). The stress statements quoted here (Hurd & Hurd 2020 = Naasioi Proper/Pirung, Darutue village; Rausch 1912 = Nasioi of the Koromira mission area) are not Oune data. Recommendation: treat oung1239 as an alias/dialect of naas1242 rather than a separate catalog entry.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: the PDF's metadata: 4 pp., A4, Acrobat PDFMaker 6.0 for Word, created 2004-08-31, real text). `extracted text` returns the heading 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length)' followed by 'Where intonation allows it, stress occurs on the first syllable of two syllable words and the second syllable of longer words.' — exactly the claimed quote, on PDF page 2, whose running header reads 'Printed: September 1, 2004 Page 2' (the header is at the top of page 2, and page 1 carries none); the text has it at lines 96-98 as stated. 'stress' occurs only on page 2 (2 hits); no other occurrence of tone/accent/pitch anywhere in the sheet, so this single sentence is the whole stress statement. the compiler p…
new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing statement for this item (Hurd & Hurd 2020 [1970], Naasioi verbs: 'first syllable of two-syllable words and on the second syllable of words of three or more syllables') and as the catalog's Naasioi [naas1242] record (weight-sensitive with a fixed default, peninitial mora per Brown 2025, where this OPD is already cited as the supporting source). One correction to the naas1242 record: its locator says 'OPD p. 3'; the stress line is on the page headed 'Page 2' (PDF page 2 of 4). The OPD describes Nasioi/Naasioi (Kieta) as a whole and names no dialect; it is not Ounge-specific.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is positional: on the second syllable of words of three or more syllables, on the first syllable of two-syllable words (i.e. peninitial with avoidance of final stress), and it is subordinate to intonation ('where intonation allows it'). The section heading lists tone and length but the sheet says nothing about tone, and it states elsewhere (p. 2, Vowels) that 'Long vowels are interpreted as sequences of two vowels' and syllabifies vowel sequences as separate syllables in the Syllable Patterns table (da.ka.na.a, o.o.an.sing, to.o.va), so 'syllable' here is effectively a vowel mora — the same counting unit Brown 2025 makes explicit for Naasioi.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the two-syllable case (initial stress) and the intonation caveat; no lexical exceptions, no nasal-onset condition (which Hurd & Hurd 1966 had mentioned), no mention of syllabic-nasal-initial disyllables.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD header reads 'Nasioi [government spelling] (Naasioi [language spelling]) Language [NAS], Kieta – North Solomons Province', data checked by Conrad Hurd (April 1992); the major-village list (Kokoree', Murumai, Ka'marove'.. Naasioi.. Oramii, Koopei..) spans several of the eight Naasioi dialect areas Hurd & Hurd name (Oramii, Koopei) but no Oune village, and no dialect is named anywhere in the sheet. Ounge/Oune is, in Conrad Hurd's own words (ISO 639-3 CR 2008-005), 'but a dialect of Naasioi', listed among the eight Naasioi dialects in Hurd & Hurd 2020 fn. 1 (Naasioi Proper/Pirung, Oune, Pakia-Si'deronsi, Oramii, Koromira, Mainoki, Daantanai', Koopei), and Tryon 2005 (p. 42) says the same. So the stress statement is for Naasioi (Naasioi Proper / Kieta) and applies to Ounge only through the dialect relationship; no Ounge-specific stress data exists in anything opened.

sources.note: Describes Nasioi of the Koromira mission / Kieta area, not Oune. p. 107 (verified against the page scan): 'Der dynamische Akzent wird im nachstehenden mit dem Zeichen ʹ kennbar gemacht. B.: kará Liebe, kára Mond, dúpui er hat es gewaschen, dupúi es ist entsprossen, puán-taansi ich habe ihn fallen getan, púantaansi ich habe „Wind entlassen“, dúmari ich habe mich gebadet, dumári ich bin nach Hause gegangen usw. In manchen zweisilbigen Wörtern stehen beide Silb…

No descriptive references at all: only Lewis 2009 (Ethnologue, a wordlist or less) and Allen & Hurd 1965: 18 (subclassification, 3 words). Alternate names Dapera, Oune, Ounge. Classification: Central Nasioi (sister of Naasioi naas1242).

sources.citation: ISO 639-3 Registration Authority. Change Request 2008-005 (submitted by Conrad Hurd, SIL, 2007-10-01; adopted 2009-01-26): rename [oue] Oune -> Ounge
sources.note: Nothing on stress. Rationale for the spelling mentions a velar nasal phoneme. Sources (a), pp. 3-4, first-hand: 'I consider Ounge to be but a dialect of Naasioi, which language I have carefully studied at close range since 1964.. I have personally visited the Oune villages, interviewed their children at the Taruruanau Catholic Mission school comparing their speech with that of other local Naasioi children, and have written a paper on Naasioi dialects, which I keep updated.. We were not party to the decision to split Ounge from Naasioi.'
